As far as I know, yes; however, there are some key points to remember when talking about changes in DNA. As far as I can remember from Genetics401 there are 2 major types of DNA changes.

  • Mutagenic: this is what you are referring to, actual physical damage and reorganization of the DNA. Here, unshielded cosmic radiation can actually tear DNA strands to shreds. This damage, however, tends to be very random and would likely lead to cancers, if not death.

  • Changes in Gene Expression: this is usually less tied in with physical damage and has more to do with your body adapting to specific circumstances. You can, for example, change which genes are being expressed in your body by things like daily meditation practices (relaxation response, etc), exercising, diet, state of mind (depression, etc), and probably a plethora of other things we haven't discovered yet.

What this article is talking about, specifically, is an elastic lengthinig of telomeres (which shortened back on earth when he came back). This doesn't really fall under the two above categories because it's not a change in the base pair sequence or even a change in the gene expression. It's a lengthening of a specific region of the DNA structure that mostly only has anything to do with cell division.

I'm kinda curious about it because I only minored in Biology, but, IIRC, telomeres are the reason we can't be immortal. Telomeres are found at the end of a DNA strand, and every time a cell undergoes division and makes a copy of its DNA for the daughter cell the telomere region of the strand is shortened (graphical representation HERE). Eventually you run out of telomere and the strand cannot copy itself anymore leading to cell death (about 50-70 divisions). I'm curios to know whether his actual telomeres simply stretched or more sequences were somehow added to the telomere region. Scientists have been trying to figure out a way to add to telomeres (or at least slow down the shortening processes) for years now.

It's still not that much more intense than say, an X-ray scan, but it's always better to be safe than sorry and things like that are cumulative.
